issues.legal_issue: The reasonable letting value of a building that has never been let and has no applicable fixed standard rent may be assessed without applying rent-control limits.
material_facts: The building had never been let on rent and was being used by its owners as a hotel.
No standard rent had been fixed for the building, and the question of fixing one did not arise.

The municipal authority assessed the building’s annual value using a reasonable letting value, and the owners challenged that assessment as exceeding the standard rent that could be fixed under rent-control law.
issues.conclusion: The municipal authority was permitted to determine the building’s reasonable letting value without regard to the rent-control provisions because the building had never been let and no standard rent had been fixed or was required to be fixed.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 138(b) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956, annual value is based on the gross annual rent at which a building might reasonably be expected to be let, notwithstanding anything in another law. If standard rent has been fixed under section 7 of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, and there is no fraud or collusion, that rent represents the reasonable letting value. But where the building has never been let and standard rent does not arise, the non-obstante clause permits assessment without applying that Act. The Court distinguished The Corporation of Calcutta v. Smt. Padma Debi, Corporation of Calcutta v. Life Insurance Corporation of India, Guntur Municipal Council v. Guntur Town Rate Payers’ Association, and New Delhi Municipal Committee v. M.N. Soi because those cases concerned let premises or statutes without the same non-obstante clause.

predicates.municipal_building_value_assessment: A municipal authority is assessing a building’s annual value for property taxation.
predicates.building_never_let: The building has never been let to a tenant.
predicates.standard_rent_not_fixed_or_applicable: No standard rent has been fixed for the building, and fixing one does not arise in the circumstances.

issues.definition: When a municipal building-value assessment concerns a building that has never been let and has no applicable fixed standard rent, the reasonable value may be determined without regard to rent-control limits.

issues.legal_issue: A municipal building valuation is not procedurally defective where the owner had an ample opportunity to be heard and relevant circumstances were considered.
material_facts: The lower appellate court’s judgment recorded that the owners’ counsel had been given ample opportunity to present their case to the municipal commissioner.
That judgment also recorded that the assessment officer had considered the relevant circumstances bearing on the building’s reasonable letting value.
The owners’ counsel did not argue before the Supreme Court that a hearing had been denied or that relevant factors had been overlooked.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to find that the owners had not received a full hearing or that the valuation was based on no principle.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the record of the lower appellate court, which showed that the owners had an ample opportunity to present their case and that relevant circumstances had been considered; the owners did not contest those matters before the Supreme Court.

predicates.municipal_building_value_assessment: A municipal authority is assessing a building’s annual value for property taxation.
predicates.owner_given_ample_opportunity: The owner was given an ample opportunity to present the owner’s case to the assessing authority.
predicates.relevant_factors_considered: The assessing authority considered the relevant circumstances bearing on the valuation.

issues.definition: If the owner had an ample opportunity to present the case and relevant valuation circumstances were considered, the assessment is not shown to be procedurally defective.
